headline: Diverse training loads improve transfer to new force histories, especially for cloth

runs.title: Same amount of training data, different load diversity
runs.scope: Each retrained shared model receives 192 extra load trajectories per material. The test scenes and load inputs are identical across all three checkpoints.
runs.summary: On two held-out waveforms, pooled response error falls from 104.2% to 89.3% for cloth and from 98.4% to 96.3% for cable compared with the same number of extra single pulses. A score of 100% matches the error from ignoring the extra load. Giving each case equal weight, the diverse cable model still averages 134.4%. The training loads match direction and peak acceleration, with different time profiles and rates. The clips show Newton, the frozen v4 model, and the diverse-load model on matched scenes.

runs.title: Shared cloth and cable under new load patterns
runs.scope: Eight fresh geometries per material, matched at six seconds. Each new force starts at 2 s at the existing load location. The gallery shows the 6 m/s² setting. The scores include 3 and 6 m/s².
runs.summary: The same frozen checkpoint was evaluated on every trajectory. Cloth's mean response error is 85–93% of the error from ignoring the added load. Cable's mean response error is 113–165% of that baseline. The added-motion score compares each rollout with its original-load counterpart after 2 s. This separates response to the extra force from the motion already under way.

runs.scope: Six-second, contact-free rollouts at 20 ms per step from clamped rest. 12 fresh cloth and 12 fresh cable scenes each have an original load schedule and a matched second-load variant.
runs.summary: The updated checkpoint uses the same recurrent architecture with more six-second training trajectories, including a second load after release, and loss measured directly in native geometry. runs.title: Does longer training reduce drift?
runs.scope: Six fresh cloth and six fresh cable scenes. The recurrent model receives the current load at each 20 ms interval.
runs.summary: Longer training improves both materials on the same six-second trajectories. Cloth drops from 11.85% to 3.61% mean error, and cable drops from 3.27% to 1.27%. The six-second test retains the original control distribution.

runs.title: Cloth and cable accuracy and speed
runs.scope: Twelve fresh cloth and twelve fresh cable scenes. Each runs 1.8 s at 20 ms intervals from the clamped rest shape under a prescribed load schedule. Position error is the mean of frame-wise all-node RMSE divided by each object's rest length. Newton targets use four substeps and eight VBD iterations.
runs.summary: The cloth and cable operators are evaluated from their initial state and the prescribed schedule. The frozen operators average 0.96% and 1.00% position error. The worst case averages 1.84% and 3.05%, respectively. The shared current-load model averages 1.79% and 1.88%. Extending its original 1.8 s fit to 6 s exposes drift. Reference refinement changes the original cable trajectory by over 20% in the paired convergence check. For moving nodes alone, mean error is 1.007% for cloth and 1.077% for cable. The compiled cloth batch takes 1.16 ms including warm scene setup. The finer cloth reference changes by up to 0.914% in mean position and 2.727% at a single frame between 32 and 64 substeps.

runs.title: OSMO checkpoint on four fresh cloth–cable scenes
runs.scope: Freeze the four-L40 checkpoint and evaluate on CPU on four new 1.8 s Newton scenes generated after model development.
runs.summary: 4 evaluated rollouts from a single 33,366-parameter checkpoint. The fit completed 400 updates using 4 GPU processes. The cable exchanges impulse with the cloth in all four scenes. Mean position RMSE is 44.13 mm with NeurALL, 45.47 mm with the analytical prior and 1.34 m with exchange disabled. Terminal cable error remains 126.40 mm and reaction-estimate error exceeds the prior.

runs.title: Training on one and four OSMO L40s
runs.scope: 400 AdamW updates on 44 checksum-matched benchmark episodes with a fixed global batch of four. Fit time includes loading scenes within the loop and excludes staging and evaluation.
runs.summary: The point-contact fit takes 87.09 seconds on one L40 and 49.88 seconds on four. The four-GPU fit is 1.75× faster and uses 2.29× as many GPU-seconds. The more expensive triangle-contact model takes 191.16 seconds on four L40s.

runs.scope: Two load-support cases and one prescribed press, 1,024 Newton MPM particles
runs.summary: The guided granular control transfers equal-and-opposite impulses. Without exchange the plate drops to the floor. With exchange it stays above the floor and the sand carries its weight, but the supported plate still sits about 3 cm too low. The press hold force is about one tenth of Newton's.

runs.title: NeurALL and Particle NeRD Local on the same scenes
runs.scope: Matched Newton references for circular push and cube pull-up
runs.summary: NeurALL has lower whole-bed error than the Particle NeRD Local retrain on both scenes. The Particle NeRD retrain has lower active velocity error on both. Damped contact has the lowest whole-bed error on both. The training runs use different data and budgets. The Particle NeRD retrain also has lower reconstructed height error near the tool on both scenes. NeurALL's geometry projection removes visible particle-center overlap at the sampled frames.

runs.title: NeurALL shared model with point contact
runs.scope: Recorded rigid motion on previously inspected public sand trajectories. Held-out Newton cloth trajectories. Held-out Newton cable trajectories. Held-out Newton mixed scenes. The coupled models exchange point-contact impulses.
runs.summary: 12 evaluated rollouts from a single 33,366-parameter checkpoint. The fit completed 400 updates using 1 CPU process. Point-contact coupling makes only a small difference for the learned rollout. The learned sand model trails the analytical baseline, and the dedicated elastic controls are substantially more accurate on cloth and cable.
